title: 'A slap in the face to us and he gets a slap on the wrist': Family angry after Toronto police officer given no jail time for assaulting a Brampton teen who later died
subtitle: Const. Calvin Au was sentenced to 12 months probation Wednesday as Chadd Facey's family watched from the public gallery.
article: The future of a Toronto police officer is in limbo after a judge spared him jail time for assaulting a teen but barred him from carrying any weapon - including his service firearm - for three years.

At the same time, seeing Const. Calvin Au walk out of the Brampton courtroom a free man on Wednesday has left the family of 19-year-old Chadd Facey struggling to find justice for their son and brother , who died of a brain bleed shortly after the assault.

Superior Court Justice Jennifer Woollcombe sentenced Au, a 34-year-old with a decade on the Toronto police force, to 12 months probation, with conditions that include he take counselling for anger management and the weapons ban. Though his defence lawyer, Peter Brauti, argued any prohibition on having a gun should come with an exception for employment, Woollcombe made the rare decision to impose the ban without exceptions - what would prevent Au from serving as a uniformed officer in Toronto or elsewhere.

"I am very concerned that despite all of his police training and experience, Au demonstrated the inability or unwillingness to assess a situation and then to use reasonable force," Woollcombe wrote in her decision. "My concerns are rooted in the safety of the public, having regard to what I find to be Au's poor judgement and inability to control himself."
Outside the courthouse, members of Facey's family said Woollcombe's decision doesn't begin to address the harm they experienced.
"I don't think it's fair because I lost my child and for him to get 12 months probation, that's not enough," said Facey's mother Fay Fagan.
His older sisters, who spoke lovingly of their brother, said they continue to be impacted by his death.
"It's like it's been a slap in the face to us and he gets a slap on the wrist," Facey's sister Nicole Hutton said. "We've been suffering."
Brauti, one of the top defence lawyers who represents Toronto police officers, told reporters they still need to review the decision but said it is possible they would file an appeal of the sentence.

The lawyer said he'd never seen a weapons ban that prohibited an officer from using his service firearm. He said it doesn't end Au's career immediately, but would be a "significant factor" for the police service to consider and hoped for a "grace period" as they contemplate an appeal.

"I'd be lying if I said I wasn't surprised at the order because this was a case that didn't involve a weapon, didn't involve a threat of a weapon," Brauti said, characterizing Au's actions as a "mistake."

Au still faces non-criminal charges at a police tribunal - a process that was paused pending the criminal trial. Brauti said it is up to the service now whether Au will remain suspended without pay, if his pay will be taken away, if he will be fired or another possible form of internal discipline.

The family earlier filed a lawsuit against Au as well as the Toronto and Peel police boards that was also put on hold during the criminal trial. The family's counsel, Asha James with Falconers LLP, said Wednesday they are ready to move ahead now with that process.

In 2021, Au had accompanied his colleague - both off duty at the time - to buy an Apple Watch from a Kijiji seller, Facey, Woollcombe found in her decision. They met the 19-year-old and exchanged $400 for a smartwatch they quickly realized was a fake. The officers chased the teen, Au on foot and Const. Gurmakh Benning in his car. Benning caught up with Facey first, who Woollcombe found had "effectively given up" after a nearly six minute pursuit.

Benning "snatched" his money back from the teen as Au approached them. Woollcombe said she couldn't be sure whether Au saw his friend recover his cash but that he had several other options, none of which involved violence. The judge noted Facey was not actively resisting, he was outnumbered and outmatched by the physically bigger men with police training.

"Unprovoked by the unarmed Facey, but still angry that this young man had got the better of them, Au failed to engage his police training to control and de-escalate the situation," Woollcombe's decision said. "Instead, he opted to use violence, running at Facey and taking him to the ground in a situation, when doing so was unwarranted, unjustified, excessive and put Facey at risk of injury."

Facey was helped home by friends where his mother saw him "clearly suffering," Fagan told the court last month as part of a victim impact statement, before being taken to the hospital where he died of a brain bleed.

Neither Au nor Benning reported the assault to Peel police or their own superiors. Once Peel police began investigating Facey's death, they learned the Toronto officers had met with the teen for the sale. The case was eventually referred to the province's Special Investigations Unit (SIU), which charged Au with manslaughter and aggravated assault a year and nine months after the assault. Benning was not charged. Weeks before the trial began, Au's charges were downgraded to just one count of assault causing bodily harm. Woollcombe convicted Au of the lesser offence of simple assault .

Reading from her sentencing decision Wednesday, Woollcombe acknowledged the devastation Facey's death caused his family as they listened from the front row of the public gallery. At times, Facey's sisters wrapped their arms around each other, comforting their grieving mother.
"It is clear to me that he was a much beloved son and brother in a close knit family," Woollcombe said.
She also spoke about the victim impact statements submitted by community groups, saying the assault on Facey "heightens the mistrust of police that exists in the Black community."
"While acknowledging that there are doubts as to the role of race in this interaction, the view expressed is that race is front and centre for Black community members," Woollcombe said.
But, the judge went on to say, it was important that Facey's death not play a role in sentencing Au for the assault, a charge that does not find him criminally responsible for the death.

The Crown had argued that Au should be sentenced to four months in jail and 12 months probation , saying it was important to appropriately sentence a law enforcement officer who breached public trust.

Au's defence lawyer, Brauti, argued a civilian would likely not be sentenced to jail time for the same offence and has said an absolute or conditional discharge - which carries no criminal record - would be more appropriate.
Woollcombe said Wednesday that granting Au a conditional discharge would have been contrary to the public interest.
"A trained officer, who purports to be acting as a police officer in effecting an arrest, breaches the public trust when he uses excessive force, even if he was off duty," Woollcombe said.
"I find these circumstances heighten the need for a sentence that denounces Au's conduct and deters others from acting in this way."

Speaking to reporters at an unrelated news conference, Toronto police Chief Myron Demkiw said he had yet to be briefed on the decision but will consider the options under the most recent laws governing discipline of officers.
